title: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, These 5 Stocks Have a History of Holding Up
detail:
If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, These 5 Stocks Have a History of Holding Up
Jennifer Saibil, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 11:20 AM CDT 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Is a market crash coming? That's the question investors are asking as the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) gets closer to ending its fourth year in a row with double-digit gains.

Understandably, a market crash is a scary thought. However, it's part of investing. When you set up your portfolio, keep that in mind and create your stock mix accordingly. When you do your annual review, swap out different stocks based on where you see gaps. And if you haven't done that yet and anticipate a market crash on the horizon, you should make your move now.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Although a market crash can affect even defensive and value stocks, some manage through better than others, and some actually thrive under adverse circumstances. Costco Wholesale (NASDAQ: COST), TJX Companies (NYSE: TJX), Coca-Cola (NYSE: KO), Procter & Gamble (NYSE: PG), and Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT) all have a history of holding up through market crashes.

What's more, they all pay dividends, and Coca-Cola, Procter & Gamble, and Walmart are Dividend Kings, meaning they've raised their dividends for at least 50 consecutive years. That's reliability under pressure. Here's how they performed in 2008, 2018, and 2022, when the S&P 500 lost value:

^SPX data by YCharts

^SPX data by YCharts

^SPX data by YCharts

1. Costco

Costco's low prices are a draw all the time, but they become even more valuable under pressure, and that's why the market loves it during a downturn. As inflation persists, rising another 3.7% in September, Costco's sales growth has accelerated, reaching 13% year over year in September.

Image source: Getty Images.

That's great news for Costco investors. Costco stock is neck and neck with the market, up 14% year to date, and if there's a correction or crash, it's likely to manage through.

Notice that in the last chart, Costco underperformed the S&P 500. However, it gained 49% the next year, nearly double the index's gain. Often, the resilience is in how quickly the stock bounces back after a downturn.

2. TJX

TJX is an off-price retail chain that buys overstock and off-season merchandise from designer brands. It works with 21,000 vendors and therefore can be very selective about what it buys.

The company sells products at 20% to 60% off retail prices in its 5,200 global stores, and it becomes a magnet for shoppers during periods of inflation or economic distress. Sales increased 4% year over year in the fiscal 2027 second quarter (ended Aug. 1), and earnings per share were up 24%.

title: 1 Red Flag That AMD Investors Should Be Aware Of Now
detail:
1 Red Flag That AMD Investors Should Be Aware Of Now
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 11:50 AM CDT 4 min read
AMD
NVDA
^GSPC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Adanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) investors have enjoyed some incredible gains during 2026. Currently, AMD is the ninth-best-performing component of the S&P 500, returning about 160% so far this year. While that figure was closer to 200% before the most recent sell-off, I think this is a wake-up call for most investors.

The reality is that AMD's stock got way too ahead of itself, and its valuation far outpaces its growth expectations. That is a major red flag for investors, and there are a few items investors need to keep an eye on as to when AMD could be a good buy again (hint: It won't be for a while).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
AMD is gaining ground, but not fast enough

The entire AMD investment thesis circles around AMD catching up to Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and taking market share. On the surface, it appears that AMD is making headway. It has huge projects like OpenAI's computing cluster, which is starting to be delivered, and is powering Meta Muse from Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META). This has all led to stronger growth for AMD, with its data center division reporting $6.7 billion in revenue and growing by 107%. Overall, this helped the company grow its revenue 50% year over year to $11.5 billion in Q2.

Those are strong results that should be celebrated, but the problem is, it just isn't enough to catch Nvidia. During Q2, Nvidia's data center revenue reached $89 billion, up 117% year over year. Overall revenue rose to $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year. While AMD appears on the surface to be doing better, the reality is that Nvidia's lead is widening.

What makes matters worse is that Nvidia's Q2 results don't include any revenue from its upcoming generation of Vera Rubin architecture chips. This new generation promises major improvements, and they also cost more than previous generations. This will further exaggerate Nvidia's lead over AMD and eliminate the thesis that AMD is catching up.

But don't tell AMD's stock that, because according to it, AMD has won the AI arms race.

AMD's stock has uncoupled from its business

Over the long term, stocks and business growth are highly correlated. Over the short term, any number of factors can influence a stock's price. This is why long-term investing is easier for individual investors, as we can afford to wait for the business results to influence the stock price as long as we've found a company with a great long-term growth thesis.

title: The Stock Market Looks Vulnerable. Should Investors Sell Their Stocks Now?
detail:
The Stock Market Looks Vulnerable. Should Investors Sell Their Stocks Now?
Lawrence Nga, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 9:43 AM CDT 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investors have reasons to worry about the stock market. On one level, hotter-than-expected inflation data renewed concerns about further Federal Reserve rate hikes. The International Monetary Fund has also warned that an artificial-intelligence-related market correction or a sharp increase in government bond yields could trigger broader financial market turmoil.

And with the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) trading close to its all-time high, one question comes to investors' minds: Should I sell before things get worse?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Personally, I wouldn't sell simply because a market crash is possible. Instead, I'd examine whether my stocks can withstand a downturn and whether their valuations leave enough room for disappointment. A market sell-off could punish speculative businesses, but it could also create opportunities to buy excellent companies at more attractive prices.

Image source: Getty Images.
Investors are concerned about the growing risks

Risk management is an important part of investing, and currently three market risks deserve investors' attention.

First, persistent inflation could keep interest rates higher for longer. Higher borrowing costs can squeeze businesses that depend on external financing, while higher bond yields can make stocks less attractive relative to bonds.

Second, the AI investment boom faces a test. Technology companies are committing enormous sums to data centers, chips, and computing infrastructure. If the resulting profits fall short of expectations, investors could reassess how much they're willing to pay for AI-related stocks.

Third, valuations matter. When investors pay a premium for future growth -- think AI stocks like Palantir Technologies or Space Exploration Technologies -- even a successful business can deliver disappointing stock returns if growth slows or investors become less willing to pay a premium.

Having said that, investors shouldn't get too carried away thinking that a crash is imminent. What they should do instead is monitor these risks over the coming weeks and make necessary adjustments to their portfolio.

Not every stock deserves the same response

Consider two companies facing the same potential market sell-off.

The first has a strong competitive advantage, recurring revenue, a healthy balance sheet, and the ability to generate cash through economic cycles. The second depends on cheap financing, burns cash, and needs continued investor support to fund its expansion. As borrowing costs rise and capital becomes harder to obtain, its financial position deteriorates.

There are lots of warning signs flashing in the stock market these days. That's causing me to shift my portfolio to a more defensive posture. I sold off several lower-conviction holdings. I'm redeploying some of the proceeds into high-quality dividend stocks.

I just invested over $4,600 across Abbott (NYSE:ABT), Procter & Gamble (NYSE:PG), and Paychex (NASDAQ:PAYX). Here's why I'm loading up on these top dividend stocks right now.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Why I'm getting defensive and investing in dividend growers

While the stock market has continued to move higher this year (the S&P 500 is up more than 13% year-to-date), there are some signs that we could be approaching a near-term top. The CAPE ratio is at its second-highest level in history, while margin debt is soaring. Meanwhile, inflation remains high, which recently led the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years. All these signs seem to point to potential for more volatility ahead.

That's leading me to shift my portfolio to a more defensive posture by adding more ballast. One of the best sources of portfolio stability without giving up long-term return potential is companies that routinely increase their dividends. According to data from Ned Davis Research and Hartford Funds, dividend growers have delivered an average annual total return of 10.2% over the last 50 years. That compares to a 4.2% annual return for dividend non-payers. Meanwhile, dividend growers have an average beta of 0.89, while dividend non-payers have an average beta of 1.18. A beta below 1.0 means a stock is less volatile than the S&P 500, while a beta above that level implies higher volatility.

A healthcare dividend stalwart

Abbott has been a stellar dividend growth stock over the years. The healthcare giant has increased its payment for 54 consecutive years, qualifying it as a Dividend King, a company with 50 or more consecutive years of annual dividend increases. Abbott hasn't just been nudging up its payment to keep its streak alive. It hiked its payout by 6.8% last year and has grown its dividend by 70% since 2020.

The diagnostics, medical devices, nutritionals, and branded-generic medicines company generates highly resilient cash flows to support its 2.4% dividend yield (more than double the S&P 500's current level of around 1%). Abbott has historically grown its earnings per share at a nearly 10% compound annual rate over the last decade, driven by organic growth and value-enhancing acquisitions. Even if Abbott grows more slowly over the next decade, it could still double an investor's money given its currently attractive valuation. The company's durable cash flows and growing dividend are just what I'm seeking these days, which is why I just bought $1,000 of Abbott stock.

title: JPMorgan Expects Q3 Earnings Growth to Broaden Beyond AI Across US and European Equities
detail:
JPMorgan Expects Q3 Earnings Growth to Broaden Beyond AI Across US and European Equities
Fiona Craig

^GSPC
NVDA
MU
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Graph showing growth ©Adobe Stock Images

JPMorgan strategists expect third-quarter corporate earnings to provide support for equity markets, citing indications that profit growth is expanding beyond artificial intelligence-related companies and across a wider range of sectors.

A team led by Mislav Matejka said earnings expectations remain elevated at the index level but become more moderate when the contribution from individual companies is excluded. The strategists believe the reporting season could shift investor attention towards corporate fundamentals following recent market volatility.

US Earnings Forecasts Reflect Significant Contributions From Technology Companies

According to IBES consensus estimates, earnings per share for the S&P 500 are expected to increase 24% in the third quarter. Estimates from FactSet and LSEG indicate growth of 30%, reflecting an adjustment for a one-off tax charge at Meta (NASDAQ:META).

Excluding Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU), expected earnings growth falls to 15%. The median S&P 500 company is projected to report an 8% increase.

In Europe, consensus forecasts indicate earnings growth of 19%, declining to 11% when energy companies are excluded. Median earnings growth is estimated at 9%, while median revenue growth stands at 7% for both the S&P 500 and the Stoxx 600.

JPMorgan said these figures suggest that earnings expectations are less demanding across the broader market than headline index forecasts indicate.

Economic Indicators Point to Continued Earnings Expansion

The bank identified improvements in global purchasing managers' indices during the third quarter, with several measures reaching multi-year highs.

JPMorgan's proprietary earnings indicator also continued to rise. According to the strategists, the indicator typically leads reported earnings by approximately two quarters, providing a basis for their expectations of continued growth over the next two reporting periods.

The team also reported that the proportion of global companies experiencing accelerating earnings growth is approaching a record level.

Although artificial intelligence remains a significant contributor to US corporate earnings, JPMorgan said profit growth is becoming more widely distributed across industries.

European Profit Margins and Sector Outlook

In Europe, JPMorgan expects operating margin expansion to contribute to earnings growth. The bank forecasts earnings before interest and taxes as a percentage of sales at 14.4% this year, approximately 250 basis points above the 2019 level.

Many investors probably feel like they missed out on Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU). The memory-chip maker's stock is up about 382% over the past year, outperforming the S&P 500's 16%.

But one reason the stock could still make new highs is simple: more of Micron's future demand is already locked in with strategic customer agreements. On the Sept. 30, 2026, earnings call, CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said, "These multi-year take-or-pay agreements sharpen our long-term supply planning and enhance the durability and predictability of our strong financial performance."

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Micron has signed 26 long-term agreements with customers. These agreements will cover more than a third of its revenue through 2030. The take-or-pay structure means customers pay whether or not they take delivery.

A large portion of high bandwidth memory -- the fast memory chips that feed data to AI chips -- is already sold out for 2027. Importantly, Mehrotra said next year's volume is commanding prices "much higher than 2026 prices."

That visibility shows up in the company's guidance. Micron expects revenue of about $61.5 billion in its current fiscal quarter, up from $54 billion in the previous quarter, with a high gross profit margin of 86%. Management expects fiscal 2027 to be another record year, with revenue growing every quarter.

Memory is a famously boom-and-bust business, and Micron is spending heavily to add capacity, so memory prices could fall if supply catches up with demand. But that's not likely to happen for at least a few more years. Mehrotra expects supply-demand conditions to be even tighter through 2028 than they were in 2026.

The stock trades at just over 5 times Wall Street's fiscal 2027 earnings estimates, as of Oct. 14, 2026. That is a low valuation for a company that analysts expect to more than double earnings per share to $176 in fiscal 2027, and increase another 17% to $206 in fiscal 2028. For investors who can tolerate a volatile stock, the positive outlook for demand and low forward P/E could support new highs over the next few years.

Intel's data center and AI segment sells the server processors that power cloud computing and AI services. Its revenue grew 59% year over year to about $6.3 billion in the second quarter. That helped drive the company's strongest revenue growth in more than 15 years.

Inference workloads are boosting orders for server CPUs, and Intel expects industry-wide server processor unit shipments to grow by strong double digits through 2027, with momentum carrying into 2028.

Intel is also bringing better products to market. It launched its first server chip, Xeon 6+, built on its new 18A manufacturing process, and 18A production is running ahead of the company's internal targets.

Relative to expected growth, the stock trades at a PEG ratio of 0.8, which looks attractive.

title: If I Only Had $1,000 to Invest, I'd Buy This 1 ETF and Wouldn't Touch It for 20 Years
detail:
If I Only Had $1,000 to Invest, I'd Buy This 1 ETF and Wouldn't Touch It for 20 Years
Neil Patel, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 4:29 AM CDT 4 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

It's hard to argue with history. In the last two decades, the S&P 500 index has delivered an annualized total return of 11.2% (as of Oct. 13). This gain shows just how powerful the stock market can be when it comes to building wealth for ordinary investors.

You might initially think that you need a sizable amount of capital to reap the rewards, but this isn't the case at all. The single most important step is to simply get started.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

It's also worth remembering some core tenets. The key is patience. Short-term swings are noise. Investors who think in decades give compounding the time it needs to work. Time in the market beats timing it.

That being said, if I were starting out with $1,000 ready to invest, I'd buy this one exchange-traded fund (ETF), and I wouldn't touch it for 20 years.

Image source: Getty Images.
Own a slice of America

There might be no ETF more popular than the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO). After all, it has a whopping $1.7 trillion in assets. This investment vehicle gives you exposure to the S&P 500 index, which contains 500 or so large and profitable U.S. companies. Investors also capture a dividend yield of 1%.

Bigger businesses have a higher weighting. The ETF's top 10 positions combine to make up a significant 38% of the portfolio. Digging deeper, Nvidia, Apple, and Microsoft represent 21% of the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF's asset base. Unsurprisingly, the information technology sector is the most prominent. Its performance has a meaningful impact.

Investors might be most drawn to the cost, though. The ETF's expense ratio sits at just 0.03%. On a $1,000 investment, this amounts to a tiny $0.30.

That kind of deal is tough to find elsewhere. There is no shortage of active funds run by expert money managers that charge exorbitant fees. Instead of outperformance, these have a poor track record of lagging the benchmark. In the world of investing, paying more rarely buys better results.

Be an optimist

Everyone might want the S&P 500's trailing-20-year performance to repeat. While that may or may not happen, there's one principle that investors must live by: Be a long-term optimist. Negative headlines get all the attention. Patience is what builds wealth.

If you plan to hold the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF over 20 years, you are almost guaranteed to make money. Extend that time horizon ever further, and the odds tilt even further in your favor.
